summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in transportation and warehousing, NAICS 48-49, at 13.0% of firms in the latest period, compared with 7.9% in the prior period. The question asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the survey first asked it in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it covers the whole sector rather than any single mode.

Where deployment is visible, it clusters in fleet operations and freight matching. Samsara describes a connected operations platform used by 20,000+ operations, with AI-driven alerts, predictive analytics, AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, automated coaching and drowsiness detection, and it credits those safety technologies with 380,000+ accidents prevented. C.H. Robinson frames its managed solutions as a move from managing logistics to autonomous logistics orchestration, where the supply chain analyzes, decides, executes and improves continuously across every shipment, and it runs an AI assistant on its site to help explore shipping options. Aurora describes self-driving freight powered by the Aurora Driver, built with hardware and software backed by verifiable AI, and quotes a partner on a hybrid model of professional drivers and the Aurora Driver hauling freight between Fort Worth and El Paso.

Aviation and maritime show the same pattern of pilots under gated rollouts. Airbus says it works with an innovation ecosystem and digitised operations toward a decarbonised, connected and autonomous future for aerospace. EASA's Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 sets out its vision for the safety and ethical considerations of AI in aviation, with an action plan, conceptual guidance deliverables and anticipated rulemaking, and EASA describes it as a living document amended once a year. The IMO adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, effective 1 July 2026, as voluntary guidance that is goal-based, technology-neutral and designed to facilitate a future transition into a mandatory instrument. The IMO states that at present there are no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships that operate autonomously or remotely controlled, though trials have shown that operation of larger remotely controlled and autonomous ships is feasible.

Money and vendor concentration sit with the equipment and platform makers. Wärtsilä positions itself as a global leader in technologies and lifecycle solutions for the marine and energy markets and points to AI-driven predictive analytics among the tools it uses to help customers decarbonise. Waymo, which began as the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and served its first fully autonomous rides in 2015, publishes a safety program and supports the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy and the Vision Zero Network. The American Trucking Associations, with more than 37,000 members and a federation of 50 state trucking associations, works to influence government policy and educate policymakers on issues affecting the industry.

On evidence and risk, the material is thinner than the marketing. Waymo's safety hub is described in this site's curated points as the most complete public evidence base from an AV operator, with published methodology and crash-rate comparisons. The IMO notes that autonomous systems and functions present different operational risks and will in many cases require an alternative approach, and that enhanced automation on its own does not make a ship a MASS or grant it privileges over conventional vessels. EASA's roadmap is explicitly human-centric and framed around safety and ethical considerations. This site's curated points add that the FAA's innovation work and EASA's AI roadmap are the regulatory record for AI flight systems, automated risk management and eVTOL certification, and that nothing flies commercially without them.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material suggests the measured base is still small, at 13.0% of transportation and warehousing firms, and that the proven ground is operational: telematics, safety monitoring, predictive maintenance, load matching and route optimization, where vendors report results in accidents prevented and cost reduction. The more ambitious autonomy plays in trucking, aviation and shipping are being rolled out under regulator-set frameworks, EASA's roadmap, the IMO's MASS Code, and the FAA and EASA gates noted in this site's curated points, so timelines depend on certification as much as on technology. The sources here report little on ROI beyond vendor claims, and the one independent measurement available is the Census Bureau's adoption share.

https://www.samsara.com/.brief: Samsara claims its connected operations platform supports more than 20,000 operations in improving safety, cutting costs, and running smarter. The platform analyzes data to provide AI-driven alerts, predictive analytics, and actionable insights that help spot risks and optimize operations. According to Samsara, its AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, automated coaching, and other safety technologies have prevented over 380,000 accidents. The system includes cameras and video AI, multicam support, driver experience tools, driver coaching, drowsiness detection, safety reporting & insights, and equipment management.

https://www.trucking.org/.brief: ATA, the American Trucking Association, says it is the largest and most comprehensive national trade association for trucking. It reports that Miguel Corral, a UPS driver, was named Bendix Grand Champion at the 2026 National Truck Driving & Step Van Championships. ATA says it has more than 37,000 members, including carriers, suppliers, shippers, and professionals, and that it works to influence government policy, educate stakeholders, and host events that bring together all parts of the industry.

https://www.wartsila.com/.brief: Wärtsilä claims it is a global leader in innovative technologies and lifecycle solutions for the marine and energy markets. The company says it already has most of the technology needed to decarbonise, from engines that can run flexibly on low- and zero-carbon fuels to AI-driven predictive analytics. Wärtsilä is using these tools to help customers take the next step on their decarbonisation journey.

https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/re.brief: The EASA has published an Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 that outlines the Agency's approach to safety and ethical considerations for AI in aviation. The roadmap provides an action plan for the EASA AI Programme, including conceptual guidance and anticipated rulemaking activities, and serves as a basis for stakeholder discussions. As a living document, it will be updated annually and refined through stakeholder exchanges and the Agency's ongoing practical work on AI development.

https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/HotTo.brief: The IMO introduced a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS Code) in May 2026, which became effective on 1 July 2026. A ship is considered a MASS only when autonomous or remote technologies replace or support crew functions and it holds a valid MASS Safety Certificate; enhanced automation alone does not qualify. The Code offers voluntary, technology-neutral guidance that complements existing regulations and defines operating conditions, limits, and responses when those limits are exceeded, creating a “goal-based framework” for safe design, operation, and certification. Trials under interim MSC 110 guidelines in June 2019 have shown that larger remotely controlled and autonomous ships are feasible, and while no SOLAS cargo ships are yet operating autonomously, the IMO anticipates commercial service in the near future with a gradual evolution toward more advanced MASS. An IMO seminar in April 2024 addressed the implications, challenges, and opportunities of MASS for ports and public authorities.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The site catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open robotics models on the Hugging Face Hub, giving each model's licence, download count and release date, and says the list is refreshed daily. It reports that the catalogue is drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page states it was last verified on 26 September 2026. It also presents itself as one part of a larger database that includes state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies, a research library, an MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests.
